extracted.intended_audience: public relations and communications professionals; PR/content writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting effective press releases that attract media attention and communicate news clearly; covers structure, style (AP), length, headlines, multimedia, SEO, and distribution considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft a headline with no more than 100 characters that uses strong action verbs to answer the question: “Why should I care?” and prompts your audience to continue reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep concise and informative; use strong, unique action verbs (e.g., 'unveil', 'reveal'); write in active voice; capitalize only the first word and proper nouns; include numbers or data to back up claims. Later guidance also suggests aiming for 70 characters or less if possible. Avoid ambiguous words, vague phrasing and jargon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the city and date showing where and when the press release was issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per AP Style: Start the first paragraph with the city in all caps, followed by the state abbreviation and the date (well-known cities may not need the state abbreviation). Example format: “NEW YORK, May 6, 2024.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead paragraph (5 Ws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a summary of the essential details in the first paragraph using the five Ws: who, what, when, where and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with the most crucial information in the first paragraph so readers/journalists immediately understand the news. This overlaps with AP Style guidance to lead with key facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body content
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand on the lead paragraph with supporting details and quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep paragraphs short, with one idea per paragraph. Provide context, background, and any necessary technical explanation while keeping flow and readability. Use supporting details to substantiate the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a quote from a relevant stakeholder or expert to add credibility and a human touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quotes to humanize the story and add authority. AP Style: use double quotation marks and introduce quotes with the speaker’s full name and title on first reference. Include quotes from someone directly affected when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide data (support claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Back up any claims with relevant statistics, survey results, historical context or industry trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using data or third-party research increases credibility and helps journalists verify claims. Use reputable sources and cite them when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call to action (CTA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a clear call to action to encourage readers to take the next step, like a link to a microsite or landing page for more details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align the CTA with the press release goal (e.g., visit website, register for event). Make next steps obvious and easy for readers and journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a brief description of the organization issuing the press release, highlighting its mission and expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep boilerplate concise and consistent across releases; include mission, core activities, and a link to the organization site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide details for media inquiries, including names, emails and phone numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include at least one contact with direct contact details so journalists can easily follow up. Ensure contact details are current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Images, video or other multimedia
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding visual elements can increase engagement with your press release, especially if you add video or images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide high-quality files or links and captions. Multimedia improves pick-up and social sharing—use images, videos, infographics where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review press release examples
rubrics_metrics.description: It's a good idea to review successful examples of press releases as a starting point for crafting your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at examples within the same industry and those with the same purpose (product launch, event, report) to model tone, structure, and angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand who your readers are: industry professionals, potential customers or a broader audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor message, language, and format to what will resonate with your target audience and how they prefer to consume information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise (word economy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stick to essential details that support your key information and avoid unnecessary jargon your audience might not understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a press release word count of 300 to 500 words to keep the message clear and focused. Edit thoroughly for grammar, style and flow; ensure each word serves a purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay relevant (why it matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell your audience why they should care about your story; make your press release timely and connected to trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect the announcement to current trends, industry developments, or broader social issues to increase pickup likelihood. Emphasize relevance in headline and lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell a story (narrative arc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write your press release like a mini-story with a clear beginning, middle and end that weaves a compelling narrative and invites curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanize the story—include quotes from people directly affected and structure content to build interest and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate SEO
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate relevant keywords, optimize headlines and descriptions and utilize backlinks to improve visibility on search engine results pages (SERPs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance SEO with journalistic readability—use relevant keywords naturally, optimize meta descriptions, and include backlinks to primary resources or landing pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide credibility (authority of sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Add authority by backing up claims with data, research or industry reports, either your own or from another reputable source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite reputable third-party sources when possible; use statistics and research to substantiate important claims and provide context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review and refine (editing and proofreading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Edit thoroughly for grammar, style and flow. First proofread to catch typos, then re-read to make sure each word serves a purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure clarity and accuracy before distribution. Confirm facts, spellings, dates, and contact details; remove jargon and excess words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release length and when to vary it
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for 300 to 500 words as a guideline, but shorter or longer releases may be appropriate depending on content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shorter (~300 words) for minor updates, time-sensitive news, or teasers. Use longer releases for complex topics, research/reports, or major announcements that require background and technical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP Style rules (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Associated Press (AP) Style, the widely used standard for journalism and press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow AP conventions to ensure clarity and journalistic compatibility. Specific AP rules called out on the page include: headline capitalization (only first word and proper nouns), dateline formatting (city in caps, state abbrev. with date), spelling/usage of numbers (spell out one-nine; use numerals for 10+; always use numerals for ages and percentages), date formats (months abbreviated when used with a date; otherwise spell out), quotes (double quotation marks; introduce speaker with full name and title on first reference), job title capitalization (capitalize only when before a name), acronyms (spell out on first use with abbreviation in parentheses), punctuation (use one space after a period; do not use the Oxford comma), and overall structure (begin with who/what/when/where/why).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution/partner selection and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing the right partner makes all the difference to getting media coverage and audience reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trusted distribution networks and reporting tools to reach relevant outlets and measure impact. Consider distribution reach, targeting, and measurement/reporting capabilities when selecting a partner.
